14 What Motivates Us Sex

Lecture 14 · What Motivates Us: Sex

Overall Summary

Sex barely registers in the time budget: Americans call it their favorite activity yet average four minutes and three seconds daily, about as much as completing IRS tax forms. In its consequences, however, it produces marriage, families, children, much aggression, competition, art, and music; without sex everything would differ. Two initial principles follow: biological facts do not entail moral conclusions, and desires shaped by selection are not commands we must obey. Genetic determination also differs from immutability: genetically caused poor eyesight is easily corrected with glasses, whereas culturally created attitudes to obesity are stubborn. Definition begins with gametes, not genitals: small male cells carry genes; large female cells add nutrition and protection. Trivers's parental-investment theory traces the ramifications. Females' minimum investment is much greater; one male can fertilize several females, leaving others mateless. Males therefore compete over quantity, developing larger bodies and weapons. Females can find mates and instead select quality, inducing male ornaments existing only for attractiveness. Emperor penguins invest equally and are similar in size; harem-competing male elephant seals are four times larger; in pipefish, males incubate and females are larger, more aggressive courters. Humans lie between: males are about 15% larger, and testes are smaller than chimpanzees' but larger than gorillas', indicating both male and sperm competition. Male violence extends from fetal kicking to prison demographics, and anonymous sex is more welcomed. Beauty signals youth and health; average faces eliminate deviations and distortions and are preferred even by babies. Empathy and mathematical-scientific differences are more contested; blue/pink swaddling, John/Joan labels, and self-segregation from four to eleven provide equally powerful social factors. Finally comes the hardest puzzle: exclusive homosexuality shows genetic predisposition, but identical-twin concordance around 50%, not 100%, requires experiential contributions. Why selection has not eliminated it remains unanswered.

Points most worth attending to:

• The gap between four minutes and three seconds and lifelong consequences redefines importance. Sex takes as little time as tax forms but generates marriage, family, aggression, competition, art, and music. Ranking importance by time is unreliable: an act matters through how extensively it changes what follows. Time and consequence budgets measure different things; the latter determines an act's place in life.

• Parental investment makes body size, aggression, and choosiness predictable and falsifiable. Male incubation in pipefish accompanies larger, aggressive, courting females; equal penguin investment accompanies similar size; harem competition gives elephant seals fourfold male size. Human testes between gorillas and chimpanzees indicate neither complete female monogamy nor unrestricted promiscuity. This intermediate state is measured, not assumed. A mechanism must risk disproof rather than remain an empty statement about sex differences.

• Same-sex behavior and exclusive homosexuality pose entirely different explanatory problems. Many animals engage in same-sex activity, which is not mysterious. The difficult question is why some men have no desire for women: selection should eliminate associated genes if carriers generally leave no offspring. Only after separating the two questions can one ask why exclusive homosexuality persists.

• About 50% identical-twin concordance is itself an argument. Pure genetic determination would imply 100% because twins are clones. Half instead requires experience, with clues pointing before puberty and perhaps prenatally. A number below the ceiling is not noise but room for experiential contributions.

Topics

Sex's Moral Weight and Why Is Does Not Imply Ought

• The lecture first dismantles two tempting inferences rather than immediately discussing sex. If desire is an adaptation for genetic propagation, same-sex, contraceptive, and postmenopausal sex do not serve reproduction and may appear unnatural. But moving from unnatural to wrong requires another premise; planes, refrigeration, and treatment of serious infections are equally unnatural. The lecturer asks that this logic be reapplied whenever an evolutionary claim appears.

• Genetic determination and immutability are logically separate. Poor eyesight is almost purely genetic, not caused by patriarchy, television, culture, or the system, yet glasses largely solve it. Conversely, attitudes to obesity are scarcely genetically constrained yet extremely resistant once culturally entrenched. Together these counterexamples separate the nature of causes from ease of reversal.

• Apply this distinction to every later sex difference. Whether a difference evolved and whether it can change are independent questions. The first answer cannot establish the second; confusing them turns “it's genetic” into a discussion-ending incantation, announcing conclusions before measurement.

How Gamete Size Explains Male Competition and Female Choosiness

• Sex is defined by gametes, not organs: many animals have neither familiar genital type. Small male cells carry genes alone; large female cells also carry food, protection, and other provisions. This difference seeds later differences and provides a truly general criterion where genitals cannot.

• The resulting mechanism is parental investment: any investment increasing an offspring's survival at the cost of investing in others. Contrast a blink producing a child with ten years' exclusive effort precluding another. Human females are constrained toward the latter because one pregnancy precludes another simultaneous one. Investment means opportunity cost, not simply effort: another offspring cannot be produced during that interval.

• Investment differences generate psychology and physiology. A male can fertilize several females, necessarily leaving some males mateless, so competition concerns number of mates. Females can find mates, making quality rather than number scarce. Males must both defeat rivals and court females; peacock plumage exists for beauty. The inference runs from gamete size through investment to mechanisms, not backward from behavior to guessed genes.

• Reversed investment provides the clearest test. Pipefish transfer eggs into the male's pouch and bloodstream while females depart; females become larger, more aggressive, and compete for males. Emperor-penguin parents both incur huge egg-protection costs, and either failure kills the egg, predicting similar size without memorizing it. Prediction before checking, rather than memorization and repetition, tests evolutionary theory's strength.

• Two measurements locate humans. Male size exceeds female size about 15%, indicating historical competition for mating opportunities. Relative testes size is below chimpanzees but above gorillas and gibbons, indicating intermediate sperm competition. This specifically suggests ancestral women were neither entirely monogamous nor indiscriminately promiscuous. Size dimorphism and intermediate testes are measurable traces of that condition.

Human Sex Differences: Violence, Anonymous Sex, and Mate Criteria

• Aggression differences begin prenatally: males kick more in utero, engage more in play fighting and combat sports, and dominate prison populations worldwide as adults, killing and injuring each other far more often. Testosterone increases aggression in humans and other primates and is not something to inject casually. Stability from prenatal kicking to prisons across ages and cultures makes innate accounts worth serious consideration.

• Receptiveness to anonymous sex is a direct investment prediction because these mechanisms predate contraception and vasectomy. Prostitution is a nearly universal male interest; pornography is universal. Duke researchers even let monkeys forgo juice to view female hindquarters or socially dominant monkey celebrities, combining People and Penthouse. Trading juice establishes a measurable cost for sexual-stimulus preferences.

• Anonymous questionnaires ask desired partner counts for next month, two years, and lifetime. Women report fewer than one for a month and four to five over two years; men's three figures are two, eight, and eighteen. Asked how long acquaintance must precede sex, women's reluctance declines with familiarity; most men accept five minutes or less. The distributions hardly overlap, motivating anonymous measurement.

• A stronger field experiment used attractive actors approaching campus strangers with invitations to go out tonight, come to an apartment, or go to bed. Over half of women accepted the first, few the second, none the third. Men's rates were about half, two-thirds, and three-quarters. The refusing quarter apologized profusely, often because a fiancée was in town. Apologetic rather than boastful refusal reveals how refusal violated their default expectations.

• Behavioral data contain a trap: heterosexual frequency compromises between different priorities and directly represents neither side's desire. Same-sex interactions offer cleaner readings. Lesbians are generally more monogamous than gay men; pre-AIDS studies recorded hundreds or thousands of male partners, described as what ordinary heterosexual men would do with equally willing women. Heterosexual frequency systematically understates male desire; same-sex samples remove that negotiation.

Beauty's Two Signals and the Average Face

• Beauty separates into youth and health signals. Youth means young but sexually mature, not preschool age: large eyes, full lips, and smooth, tight skin. Health appears in absence of deformity, clear eyes, unblemished skin, and intact teeth. These bodily cues make attractiveness identifiable rather than purely subjective.

• Averaging is a filter. Deformities deviate from the average, so superimposing faces cancels deviations and distortions. Faces become more asymmetrical with age, while averages have no asymmetrical location. Combining many faces smooths every possible place for things to go wrong.

• Evidence includes a proposed classroom photo composite, which would produce a very attractive face. In a sequence of increasingly averaged Caucasian faces, most see rising attractiveness. The subtle effect nevertheless makes infants look longer at averages, suggesting preference precedes culture. Babies have had no opportunity to learn beauty standards, excluding the cultural account here.

• Averaging is not the endpoint. Further feminizing prototype features yields a more sexually cued, preferred face. Broadening and squaring an average male jaw and chin contrasts two attractive types: youthful, healthy, strong-looking good provider versus hot, apparently good genes. Most prefer the former, but three laboratories replicated ovulating women's preference for the latter. This physiological-state exception shows preferences can be temporarily adjusted upward or downward.

• Cross-cultural mate commonalities also matter. Among 10,000 respondents in thirty-seven countries, kindness and intelligence rank highly for dates, spouses, and sexual partners. Women emphasize power, status, and willingness to invest in children; men emphasize fertility. Reproductively, male age matters less than female age: twenty versus fifty radically changes women's capacity to bear children. Commonalities concern valued qualities; differences concern each sex's priorities.

Another Source of Sex Differences: Social Treatment and Self-Segregation

• Some differences have less clear origins than aggression and mate preference, and social factors are at least equally powerful. Adults treat the same baby differently when blue-swaddled and called a boy versus pink-swaddled and called a girl. Identical emails, applications, and manuscripts elicit different expectations when signed John Smith or Joan Smith. Changing names changes outcomes, showing treatment produces rather than merely reflects differences.

• Many experience this directly: men with apparently female names, women with apparently male names, or people whose names are gender-ambiguous to Western ears encounter “Oh, you're a man; now I'll treat you differently.” Accumulated everyday treatment is central to social explanations. Each shift is small, but cumulatively can shape self-expectations.

• Gender self-segregation amplifies differences, typically from four to eleven. Boys group with boys and girls with girls. Eleanor Maccoby proposes that initially slightly greater male aggression is reinforced and exaggerated in boys' groups, while girls' nonaggression is amplified differently. This interval provides a window converting small initial differences into substantial ones.

• Empathy and mathematical-scientific ability are most controversial. Innate female-empathy accounts cite greater male violence, murder as extreme empathy failure, testosterone's association with lower sociability, slightly lower male empathy, and somewhat poorer social-cognition/theory-of-mind performance, though disputed. The clearest sex difference is male predominance in autism, Asperger's, conduct disorder, and psychopathy. Correlation does not settle causes; the class explicitly questions whether this reflects innate mechanisms or social expectations.

• Competing materials address innate mathematical-scientific differences. A former Harvard president suggested women's underrepresentation in engineering and science reflects intrinsic aptitude, especially variability. He accepted equal averages but proposed a wider male distribution, producing more very poor performers and geniuses. Rather than adjudicate this controversial claim in one sentence, the lecturer refers listeners to Pinker and Spelke's public debate. Withholding an instant verdict means the issue needs a full debate, not a slogan.

Sexual Orientation: Predisposition, Necessary Experience, and Evolutionary Puzzle

• Distinguish orientation from behavior. Same-sex acts can reflect boredom, experimentation, or other reasons. The question is not what one has done but, all else equal, what kind of person one wants sexually or romantically. Most are heterosexual; bisexuality estimates vary culturally. Exclusive homosexuality is the difficult target requiring evolutionary explanation once behavior is separated from desire.

• Some explanations can nearly be excluded. Orientation is not conscious choice: under severe discrimination or even personal moral disapproval, few would voluntarily select homosexuality. Seduction after puberty also seems unlikely because sexual and romantic fantasies reveal orientation's seeds earlier, though such studies need caution. Both arguments suggest orientation is given rather than chosen.

• Standard behavioral genetics finds partial heredity. Identical/fraternal and adopted/biological sibling comparisons reveal genetic predisposition to homosexuality. But identical concordance is about 50%, much above population prevalence and far below 100%. Pure heredity would make clones fully concordant. Experience must therefore contribute, perhaps prenatally. Here behavioral genetics uses a logical ceiling not merely to estimate proportions but to direct inquiry toward early experience.

• The puzzle is not male-male sex, explicable through recreation or bonding, but some men's lack of desire for women and some women's lack of desire for men. Selection would appear to eliminate associated tendencies because carriers generally leave no offspring without modern technology. Stable persistence without offspring requires an additional evolutionary explanation.

Questions: What Cross-Species Data Can Tell Us About Orientation's Origins

• A student asks about comparable other-species data, directly constraining any origin theory. Many animals have same-sex interactions, so such behavior is neither rare nor itself mysterious. Cross-species evidence draws a boundary around what needs explanation.

• Missing data concern exclusivity: the proportion of nonhuman primates not wanting opposite-sex sex is unknown. If exclusivity is human-only, its persistence remains a specifically human evolutionary puzzle. Without that proportion, human-origin accounts lack a crucial comparison.

Key Quotations

"Nature does not dictate what we should accept or how we should live our lives."

Before moral discussion, this denies direct inference from evolution to what we should accept or how to live.

"By Darwinian standards, I am a horrible mistake, a pathetic loser, but I am happy to be that way, and if my genes don't like it they can go jump in the lake."

An evolutionary scholar's joke about voluntary childlessness shows Darwinian failure can still be a good life.

"Nothing moral necessarily follows from the facts of biology."

The central moral principle precedes discussion of inevitability.

"Genetic causes and environmental causes are in principle no different from each other. Some may be harder to reverse, others may be easy."

Separating causes and reversibility prepares discussion of mutability and rejects genes as inescapable destiny.

"It's biologically caused but fairly easy to fix."

Poor eyesight completes the argument: genetically caused conditions can be corrected with glasses.

"It is based on an idea by Robert Trivers called "parental investment.""

The explanatory engine from which size, aggression, and choosiness predictions follow.

"Females, barring technological advance, have a huge investment into any offspring;"

Investment differences are structural constraints, not preferences: pregnancy precludes another simultaneous pregnancy.

"Males — and a single male could fertilize several females, forcing some males to go mate-less and giving rise to competition to see who can mate with the most females."

The key move from investment to psychological mechanisms explains male competition.

"Same hen every time?" The guy says, "No, different hen every time." And he says, "Tell that to Mrs. Coolidge."

The Coolidge Effect punch line introduces sex differences in preference for sexual variety.

"In this study, the twenty five percent of males who said "no" apologized profusely, and they said, "Oh, you know, my fiancé's in town, and [unintelligible].""

A field-experiment detail depicts men's discomfort in refusing these offers.

"what these gay men are doing is exactly what your average heterosexual man would do if he had that degree of willing females who were as willing as he was."

Same-sex data reveal desire more directly than heterosexual frequency, which compromises between priorities.

"Average-ness seems to factor out all the bad things that could happen."

Averaging cancels deviations and distortions, explaining attractive averages.

"These two people don't exist. They're computer composites."

The perfect displayed faces have no corresponding real people.

"To be a man is to suffer from a particularly mild form of autism."

A reported slogan summarizes the claim of relatively weaker male social cognition.

"So, your reading response for this week is "solve that puzzle.""

The unexplained evolutionary origin of exclusive homosexuality becomes the assignment.

Novel Ideas

• Evolutionary origin and mutability are independent questions — Genetically caused poor eyesight is easy to correct, cultural obesity attitudes hard to change. These examples overturn genes-as-destiny and establish two tracks for every difference: evolutionary origins do not imply immutability or vice versa. Separating axes prevents evolutionary claims becoming fatalism.

• Sex is temporally minor and causally pervasive — Four minutes and three seconds, comparable to tax forms, generates marriage, children, aggression, competition, art, and music. Time fails as importance's measure, explaining sex's place under what motivates us. Temporal insignificance and consequential pervasiveness coexist.

• Average faces are beautiful because averaging cancels defects — Beauty is not usually associated with mediocrity, yet composites resemble no particular person and look best. Deformities deviate; averaging cancels deviations. Infants' longer looking suggests precultural preference. An ordinary statistical operation produces faces judged most beautiful.

• Same-sex data give cleaner desire readings — Heterosexual frequency negotiates competing priorities and reflects neither party directly. Same-sex couples remove that compromise. Pre-AIDS extreme male partner counts indicate what heterosexual men might do with equally willing women. Purity depends on how much negotiation is removed.

• About 50% twin concordance is a conclusion, not noise — Beyond supporting genetic contribution, it gives a stronger inference: clones should be 100% concordant if genes wholly determined orientation, so experience must contribute, with clues before puberty or prenatally. Read this way, an imperfect figure becomes positive evidence about experience rather than insufficiency.

• Reversed-investment species permit advance predictions — Equal penguin care predicts equal size without memorization. Theory's strength lies not in retrospectively explaining fourfold elephant-seal dimorphism but in predicting similar gibbon and penguin sizes. Advance prediction earns the label explanation, a recurring classroom criterion.

Counterintuitive Ideas

• Common sense says: A favorite activity must consume much time. → In fact: Sex averages four minutes and three seconds daily, like IRS paperwork. Importance cannot be inferred from duration.

• Common sense says: Genetic traits are unchangeable. → In fact: Genetic poor eyesight is easily corrected, culturally produced obesity attitudes stubborn. Cause and reversibility are independent axes.

• Common sense says: Male size and strength are self-evident. → In fact: Females produce larger gametes; humans' 15% male size advantage traces mating competition, while male-incubating pipefish have larger, aggressive, courting females.

• Common sense says: Beauty is ineffable and subjective. → In fact: Youth and health supply identifiable universal cues—eyes, lips, skin, lack of deformity, teeth—and averaging cancels deviations, attracting even infants.

• Common sense says: Equal mean ability implies equal genius distributions. → In fact: The contested aptitude claim concerns variability rather than means: greater male spread would yield more extreme failures and geniuses. The issue is referred to Pinker and Spelke's debate.

• Common sense says: Homosexuality is a lifestyle choice, or at least optional. → In fact: Gay people may face severe discrimination and moral self-disapproval without being able to choose, and orientation appears in prepubertal fantasies. Choice accounts conflict with these facts.

Core Tensions

Biological facts and moral conclusions

• One side: Desire serves gene propagation; nonreproductive same-sex, contraceptive, and postmenopausal sex do not, appearing unnatural and therefore easily labeled wrong.

• The other side: Unnatural does not entail wrong, or flight, refrigeration, and surviving infection would be wrong. Reproduction-only morality would exclude contraception. Evolved brains can choose their destinies.

• Resolution: The lecturer explicitly concludes “Nothing moral necessarily follows from the facts of biology,” asking listeners to reapply it to every later evolutionary claim.

Evolutionary determination and mutability

• One side: Selected differences seem built into mechanisms and difficult to remove, making proposed change appear premature.

• The other side: Genetic and environmental causes differ in reversibility individually, not in principle. Poor eyesight is genetic and easy; body-size attitudes are cultural and hard. Treating genes as fate is near-astrological nonsense.

• Resolution: This is a logical distinction, not an empirical answer. Causes and reversal are separate questions, requiring measurement for each difference; no specific reversal difficulty is established.

Innate differences and social amplification

• One side: Cross-cultural aggression, preferences, and anonymous-sex attitudes are strong biological-adaptation candidates. Empathy and autism sex ratios also support innate hypotheses.

• The other side: Swaddling color, John/Joan labels, and self-segregation from four to eleven create and amplify differences. The lecturer is explicitly quite skeptical about biology's share in these contested cases.

• Resolution: Unresolved and debatable. The lecturer leans toward social explanations and declines a verdict on aptitude, referring to Pinker and Spelke.

Same-sex behavior and exclusive homosexuality: different puzzles

• One side: Same-sex behavior is common in animals and can be recreational or affiliative, requiring no special explanation.

• The other side: Exclusive orientation removes opposite-sex desire and usually offspring without modern technology, apparently inviting elimination by selection.

• Resolution: Explicitly open. Behavioral genetics establishes predisposition and necessary experience through 50% concordance, but neither the experiences nor persistence is explained. The problem becomes the reading assignment.

Methodology

• Parental-investment inference: Derive minimum investment, mating competition, size, and aggression from gamete differences, then test species with reversed investment.

◦ Step 1: Identify the large-gamete sex and minimum pregnancy, incubation, lactation, and childcare opportunity costs.

◦ Step 2: Predict low-investment competition for mate quantity and high-investment selection for mate quality.

◦ Step 3: Predict size, weapons, ornaments, aggression, and courtship initiative; reverse predictions with investment reversals.

◦ Step 4: Check elephant seals with fourfold males, similar-sized monogamous gibbons, equal-investment penguins, and male-incubating pipefish with larger aggressive females.

• Anonymous questionnaires on desire: Ask partner counts over time and acquaintance thresholds anonymously, bypassing both “everyone knows” and “that's sexist” reactions.

◦ Step 1: Ask desired partners next month, two years, and lifetime.

◦ Step 2: Compare distributions, not just means, by sex.

◦ Step 3: Ask required acquaintance from a year or six months down to a week or five minutes and observe distribution shifts.

• Field experiments on sexual offers: Replace reports with requests at three intimacy levels to compare acceptance.

◦ Step 1: Recruit attractive outside actors to avoid acquaintance effects.

◦ Step 2: Approach strangers with standardized attraction statements and one invitation: go out, come to the apartment, or go to bed tonight.

◦ Step 3: Record acceptance by sex, plus refusal styles and reasons as qualitative evidence.

• Same-sex sample readings: Where heterosexual behavior compromises between priorities, use same-sex data to read each side's desire more directly.

◦ Step 1: Recognize heterosexual frequency as negotiated rather than a direct desire index.

◦ Step 2: Compare gay men's and lesbians' partner counts and monogamy.

◦ Step 3: Note messy survey data but consistent direction across studies.

• Face averaging: Combine faces computationally, test attractiveness against averaging, and use infant looking to exclude cultural explanations.

◦ Step 1: Collect many same-population photos and generate differing degrees of averaging.

◦ Step 2: Have adults rate increasing averages and test monotonic attractiveness gains.

◦ Step 3: Compare infant looking at averaged and unaveraged faces; average preference indicates a precultural tendency.

◦ Step 4: Feminize averages or exaggerate square jaws and test changes beyond the average, including ovulation-related preference shifts.

• Standard behavioral-genetic separation for orientation: Compare twin concordance and adopted/biological siblings to estimate genetic contributions.

◦ Step 1: Compare monozygotic and dizygotic concordance; differences indicate genetic contribution.

◦ Step 2: Compare adopted and biological siblings to separate shared environments and genes.

◦ Step 3: Check the logical ceiling: pure heredity predicts concordance of one, while about 50% requires experience and directs inquiry toward prenatal or other early experiences.

Key Data

• Four minutes and three seconds — Context: Average daily American sex time, comparable to tax paperwork despite ranking sex as favorite.

• 97%, 98%, 99% — Context: Difficult estimates of female attraction to males, with 98% used provisionally.

• 96% — Context: Male attraction to females, likewise uncertain and variable.

• 15% — Context: Average male size advantage, evidence for historical mating competition.

• About 50%, one-half — Context: A gay person's identical twin's likelihood of also being gay, above prevalence but below genetic determinism's 100%.

• Partner counts at three timescales — Context: Women report fewer than one and four to five across month, two-year, and lifetime questions; men about two, eight, eighteen.

• One year / six months / a week or less — Context: Women's acquaintance thresholds with desirable partners: yes, unsure, no.

• Five minutes — Context: The threshold a majority of men accept.

• 50% / 69% / 75% — Context: Men's acceptance of going out, apartment visits, and sex tonight.

• Over half / very few / none — Context: Women's acceptance in the same three conditions.

• 25% — Context: Men refusing, often apologetically because fiancées were in town.

• 10,000 people, thirty-seven countries — Context: Cross-cultural preferences for dates, spouses, and sexual partners.

• Four times — Context: Male elephant-seal size in winner-take-all harem competition.

• Ages four to eleven — Context: Approximate gender self-segregation interval, varying culturally.

• Three laboratories — Context: Replications of ovulating women's preference for exaggerated masculine jaw/chin features.

• Over a hundred or a thousand partners — Context: Pre-AIDS male same-sex survey figures, not found at comparable levels among women.

• About a year earlier — Context: Harvard's Pinker-Spelke debate posted on Edge, identified in course materials as the 2005 debate.

English

Equivalent

parental investment

Trivers's investment in offspring survival at the cost of investing in other offspring; the core explanatory engine.

sex cell / gamete

sex cell / gamete

Male small sperm carry genes; female large eggs add food and protection, defining sex without genitals.

Coolidge Effect

Named for the presidential farm story, increased male interest in novel partners, supporting sexual-variety preferences.

sexual choosiness

Selectivity about partners; investment theory predicts greater female selectivity and male anonymous-sex acceptance.

sperm competition

Competition in sperm production with multiply mating females; intermediate human testes imply intermediate competition.

Successive time-limited pair bonds in American culture, potentially lifelong but usually not, rather than lifelong monogamy.

Increasing facial asymmetry over time, a deviation from the average underlying the attractiveness account.

Understanding others' mental states; used in contested innate-female-advantage claims and autism-ratio explanations.

An empathy/social-cognition disorder grouped with autism, more common in males and cited for innate differences.
